title: THEY THREW THEIR BROTHER INTO A PIT — YEARS LATER, THEY BOWED BEFORE HIM BEGGING FOR FOOD
paragraphs: THEY THREW THEIR BROTHER INTO A PIT — YEARS LATER, THEY BOWED BEFORE HIM BEGGING FOR FOOD
They thought they were burying Joseph’s future. They had no idea God was writing a rescue story through the very man they betrayed.
There are wounds caused by strangers.
And then there are wounds that know your name.
Wounds that sat at your table.
Wounds that grew up in the same house.
Wounds with familiar faces.
Joseph knew the difference.
The men who stripped him, threw him into a pit, and eventually sold him were not foreign enemies.
They were his brothers.
His own blood.

And years later, when famine emptied their fields and hunger drove them into Egypt, those same brothers would stand before Joseph needing something from the man they once decided they could live without.
Food.
But before we rush to that extraordinary reversal, we need to stand beside the pit.
Because somebody reading this knows what it feels like to be there.
Not literally.
But emotionally.
You know what it is to discover that someone you trusted could hurt you.
You know what it is to replay a betrayal at two in the morning and wonder how someone who knew your heart could treat it so carelessly.
You know what it is to watch people continue living normally after what they did nearly destroyed you.
And perhaps the hardest question has not been, “Why did they do this?”
Perhaps it has been:
“God… where were You?”
Joseph's story does not insult that question with an easy answer.
It takes us into the pit first.
Genesis 37:24 records the moment in stark Hebrew:
וַיִּקָּחֻהוּ וַיַּשְׁלִכוּ אֹתוֹ הַבֹּרָה וְהַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם
Vayyiqqachuhu vayashlikhu oto habborah; vehabbor req, ein bo mayim.
“They took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.”
The Hebrew word בּוֹר — bor means a pit or cistern.
Notice how brutally simple Scripture is.
They took him.
They threw him.
The pit was empty.
No water.
No inspirational speech appears from heaven.
No angel immediately lifts Joseph out.
No explanation arrives telling him how everything will eventually work.
Just darkness.
And that matters.
Because sometimes we retell Joseph's story so quickly that we accidentally remove its pain.
We know the ending.
Joseph didn't.
We know Egypt is coming.
Joseph didn't.
We know Pharaoh is coming.
Joseph didn't.
We know the palace is coming.
Joseph didn't.
We know his brothers will one day bow before him.
Joseph didn't.
Inside the pit, Joseph had only the pit.
And faith becomes painfully real when you cannot see the next chapter.

His brothers had already hated him because of his father's favoritism and because of the dreams Joseph reported. They saw him coming and conspired against him. They stripped away the special robe his father had given him.
Imagine that moment.
The hands pulling the robe from Joseph's body belonged to men he had called brothers.
Then they threw him down.
And while Joseph was trapped, something almost unbearable happened.
They sat down to eat.
The people responsible for his terror could still swallow their lunch.

Later, when famine brought those brothers before Joseph, they remembered what happened far more vividly than Genesis 37 initially tells us. Genesis 42:21 records their confession: they remembered seeing the distress of Joseph's soul and hearing him plead with them.
Joseph had begged.
They had heard him.
And they refused to listen.
That changes the emotional temperature of the pit.
This was not a silent teenager stoically accepting his destiny.
This was a brother crying out to brothers.
Please.
Help me.
Don't do this.
And they did it anyway.
Maybe that is why this story reaches places inside us that polished Christianity sometimes cannot.
Because some of you prayed while somebody was hurting you.
You asked God to change the situation.
You begged someone to reconsider.
You hoped the marriage would heal.
You hoped the friendship would survive.
You hoped the family member would finally acknowledge what happened.
You hoped the person who betrayed you would come back and make it right.
But the footsteps disappeared.
And you were left wondering whether God had disappeared with them.
He hadn't.
That is one of the great truths of Joseph's story.
God's silence is not God's absence.
Joseph was taken from the pit and sold into slavery. He eventually entered the household of Potiphar in Egypt. Scripture repeatedly emphasizes that the LORD was with Joseph.
Not merely after Joseph became successful.
With him there.
In slavery.
Then came another injustice.

Potiphar's wife attempted to seduce Joseph. Joseph refused, grounding that refusal not merely in loyalty to Potiphar but in loyalty to God. He asked how he could commit such wickedness and sin against God.
Joseph chose integrity.
And his immediate reward was prison.
Read that again slowly.
He did the right thing…
and his circumstances became worse.
That destroys one of the most dangerous counterfeit versions of Christianity: the idea that obedience guarantees immediate comfort.
Sometimes obedience costs you.
Sometimes telling the truth costs you.
Sometimes refusing temptation costs you.
Sometimes doing what honors Christ does not immediately open a door.
Sometimes it appears to slam one shut.
Joseph went from pit…
to slavery…
to false accusation…
to prison.
If you stopped reading there, you might conclude that Joseph had been abandoned.
But heaven was still writing.
Even in prison, God was with him.
Eventually Joseph interpreted dreams for Pharaoh's officials. One of those men, the cupbearer, was restored to his position.
Joseph asked to be remembered.
But he was forgotten.
Again.
Have you ever survived betrayal only to be wounded by being forgotten?
You helped people who disappeared when you needed help.
You poured into people who stopped checking on you.
You celebrated people who never celebrated you.
You thought, “Maybe this person is the answer God sent.”
Then nothing.
Joseph waited.
Until Pharaoh dreamed.
And suddenly the gift that seemed useless inside a prison became necessary inside a palace.
Joseph was summoned.
God enabled Joseph to explain that Egypt was approaching seven years of extraordinary abundance followed by seven devastating years of famine. Joseph proposed wise preparation.
Pharaoh recognized something extraordinary in him and elevated the former Hebrew slave to enormous authority over Egypt.
Think about the reversal.
The boy stripped of his robe was clothed in authority.
The brother thrown into a pit was lifted beside Pharaoh.
The slave became an administrator.
The prisoner became the man entrusted with grain.
But do not reduce Joseph's story to “suffer now and God will make you rich later.”
That is not the Gospel.
The deepest miracle is not that Joseph received a position.
It is what God did through Joseph's suffering to preserve life—and what God did inside Joseph's heart.
Because then the famine came.
And eventually…
so did his brothers.
The men who once looked down into a pit at Joseph now bowed down before him.
They did not recognize him.
Joseph recognized them.
Imagine the emotional collision.
One glance…
and suddenly the pit is back.
The voices.
The robe.
The pleading.
The merchants.
The journey away from home.
Years of separation from his father.
Joseph now possessed something his younger self never had.
Power.
He could punish them.
He could expose them.
He could make them experience a fraction of what he had experienced.
And nobody in Egypt would have stopped him.
This is where we discover whether Joseph merely escaped the pit…
or whether God had begun removing the pit from Joseph.

The story unfolds carefully. Joseph tests his brothers, and Scripture shows that they are no longer the same men who sold him. Judah, who had once participated in Joseph's sale, eventually offers himself in place of Benjamin rather than allow their father to suffer the loss of another beloved son.
Something has changed.
Then Joseph can no longer contain himself.
Genesis 45 says he ordered everyone else out of the room.
And Joseph wept.
Not a dignified little tear.
He wept so loudly that Egyptians heard him and Pharaoh's household heard about it.
Years of history erupted through one man's chest.
Then came the words his brothers could never have expected.
“I am Joseph.”
Imagine their faces.
The brother they sold.
Alive.
Standing before them.
Powerful.
Their survival now resting in the hands of the man whose cries they had once ignored.
They were terrified.
And then Joseph did something astonishing.
He invited them closer.
“Come near to me.”
Then he identified the wound without pretending it never happened:
“I am your brother Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.”
That sentence matters.
Forgiveness did not require Joseph to rewrite evil as good.
He named what they did.
You sold me.
Biblical forgiveness is not pretending betrayal was harmless.
It is not calling abuse love.
It is not denying consequences.
It is not automatically restoring trust without repentance, wisdom, or boundaries.
Joseph could acknowledge human evil while simultaneously recognizing divine providence.
He continued by explaining that God had sent him ahead to preserve life.
Later, after Jacob died and Joseph's brothers again feared retaliation, Joseph gave one of Scripture's clearest statements about God's providence over human evil.
Genesis 50:20 says:
וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Ve'attem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah.
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
The repeated Hebrew verb comes from חָשַׁב — chashav, carrying the sense of thinking, planning, reckoning, or intending.
Do not miss the force of the sentence.
Joseph did not say:
“What you did wasn't evil.”
He said it was evil.
Human responsibility remained real.
But human evil did not become sovereign.
They intended one thing.
God intended another.
Same history.
Different intentions.
They were not secretly doing God's righteous work when they betrayed Joseph. Their motives were sinful.
Yet their sin was incapable of overthrowing God's purpose.
That is biblical providence.
God does not need evil to become good in order to defeat it.
He is so sovereign that evil cannot ultimately force Him to surrender His purposes.
The pit did not become good.
The betrayal did not become good.
Slavery did not become good.
False accusation did not become good.
Prison did not become good.
God remained good.
And He brought saving purposes through circumstances other people intended for destruction.
That distinction matters enormously, especially for wounded people.
Christianity never requires you to look at what destroyed pieces of your life and call darkness light.
You can say:
“That was wrong.”
“That hurt me.”
“They betrayed me.”
“I still have scars.”
And at the same time say:
“But Jesus will not allow my wound to become my god.”
Maybe this is where Joseph's story stops being ancient history and starts reading your mail.
Because perhaps someone threw you into a pit years ago, and although your body climbed out, your heart still lives there.
Every new relationship gets interrogated for the crimes of the old one.
Every disagreement feels like abandonment.
Every silence sounds like rejection.
Every memory reopens court.
You survived what happened…
but what happened is still governing you.
And Jesus wants more for you than survival.
He wants freedom.
Forgiveness does not mean the offender was right.
Forgiveness means you refuse to let their sin become the permanent owner of your soul.
And here the road from Joseph leads us toward Someone greater than Joseph.
Jesus Christ.
Joseph is not Jesus, and we should not force every detail of Joseph's life into an allegory. But Scripture's great redemptive story ultimately moves toward Christ, and there are striking resonances.
Joseph was rejected by his brothers.
Jesus “came to His own,” and His own did not receive Him.
Joseph was handed over and sold.
Jesus was betrayed for silver.
Joseph suffered despite innocence.
Jesus was perfectly sinless and nevertheless condemned.
Joseph descended into humiliation and later was exalted.
Christ humbled Himself to death—even death on a cross—and God highly exalted Him.
Joseph's suffering became part of God's means of preserving lives during famine.
But Jesus went infinitely further.
He did not merely preserve starving people with grain.
He gives eternal life to sinners who deserve judgment.
At the cross, humanity's deepest scandal collided with God's astonishing grace.
Men crucified the Son of God.
And through that very cross, according to God's sovereign redemptive purpose, Christ bore sin and opened the way of forgiveness for everyone who repents and believes.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately a message about becoming powerful enough that your enemies someday need you.
It is about Christ being merciful enough to save His enemies.
That includes us.
Before pointing at Joseph's brothers, remember:
Sin makes rebels of all of us.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Envied.
Hated.
Hidden.
Manipulated.
Worshiped ourselves.
Ignored God.
Excused what He calls sin.
Some sins are public.
Others wear church clothes.
But every one of us needs grace.
The most shocking part of the Gospel is not merely that Jesus was betrayed.
It is that Jesus willingly died for sinners.
Romans tells us that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
You may have spent years asking, “How could they do that to me?”
There is another question that eventually brings every human heart to its knees:
“How can a holy God show mercy to me?”
The answer is Jesus.
Not your religious résumé.
Not your charitable deeds.
Not the image you maintain online.
Not the verses you repost while hiding the sins you refuse to surrender.
Jesus.
Crucified.
Risen.
King.
The Gospel does not tell you to decorate your pit.
It calls you out of it.
Repent.
Stop making peace with the sin Christ died to save you from.
Stop confusing conviction with condemnation. Conviction points you toward the Savior.
Bring the secret thing into the light.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the pride.
Bring the affair.
Bring the envy.
Bring the unforgiveness.
Bring the religious performance.
Bring the anger you have fed for years.
Bring the wound you turned into an identity.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to come near.
That may be the most beautiful echo in Joseph's story.
When the guilty brothers were terrified, Joseph said:
Come near.
And the Gospel announces something even greater to repentant sinners.
Come to Christ.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because justice does not matter.
Because at Calvary, justice and mercy meet in the crucified Savior.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something nobody around you knows.
Maybe you are Joseph, wounded by people you trusted.
Maybe you are one of the brothers, haunted by something you did years ago.
Maybe you are both.
Wounded…
and guilty.
Betrayed…
and betrayer.
That is where grace becomes more than a Christian vocabulary word.
Grace means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming people inside the scandal.
Joseph's brothers could not undo the pit.
Joseph could not recover the stolen years.
But God could still write redemption into a family stained by jealousy, deception, betrayal, and grief.
And from that deeply imperfect family line, God's covenant purposes continued until, generations later, the promised Messiah came.
Jesus Christ.
So maybe the question is no longer:
“Why did God let me enter the pit?”
Maybe tonight the question is:
“What if the pit does not get the final word?”
What if the betrayal that changed you does not have to define you?
What if the person who abandoned you does not get to decide your capacity to love?
What if the failure you are ashamed of does not have to become the name you answer to forever?
What if repentance is still possible?
What if forgiveness is still possible?
What if restoration is still possible?
What if God has been present in chapters where you were certain He had left?
Joseph looked backward and saw something his younger self could never have seen from inside that empty cistern.
God had not surrendered the story.
Neither had He excused the evil.
He had overruled it.
That is why Genesis 50:20 is not a motivational slogan promising that every Christian will become wealthy, influential, famous, or publicly vindicated.
It is far better than that.
It tells us that evil is not sovereign.
God is.
And for those who belong to Christ, suffering cannot separate us from the love of God.
Sometimes God changes circumstances.
Sometimes He changes us while the circumstances remain painful.
Sometimes earthly reconciliation happens.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
Sometimes justice comes quickly.
Sometimes we wait for the final judgment of the perfectly righteous King.
But Christians never have to pretend evil wins.
The empty tomb has already announced otherwise.
Jesus Christ walked into death itself…
and walked out alive.
So if you are in a pit right now, do not worship the darkness.
If you are waiting, do not assume waiting means abandonment.
If you have been betrayed, do not let another person's sin teach your heart to become sinful.
If you have betrayed someone, stop hiding behind excuses. Repent. Confess where appropriate. Make restitution where possible. Seek forgiveness.
And if you are exhausted from carrying bitterness, place judgment into the hands of the only Judge who sees every detail perfectly.
You do not have to become what hurt you.
Joseph didn't.
And by the transforming grace of Jesus Christ, neither do you.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't perform for anybody.
Be honest.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession is the moment somebody finally stops hiding, and another believer realizes they are not fighting alone.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Not because sharing proves your faith.
Not because an algorithm glorifies God.
But because the Gospel is worth carrying beyond ourselves.
Someone may believe betrayal has destroyed their future.
Someone may be drowning in guilt over what they did years ago.
Someone may be one sentence away from remembering that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Send it to them.
Because Joseph's story leaves us with an image difficult to forget:
The brothers who once stood above Joseph while he lay helpless in a pit eventually stood helpless before Joseph.
But the greatest reversal was not that Joseph finally had power over them.
It was that when revenge became possible…
mercy was still alive inside him.
And that points our eyes beyond Joseph.
Toward Jesus.
The King before whom every knee will ultimately bow is the same Savior who stretched His hands upon a cross and offers forgiveness to repentant sinners today.
So bring Him the pit.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the years.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the guilt.
Bring Him the scandal.
And bring Him the pieces of yourself you thought could never become anything beautiful again.
Because the hands of Christ still bear scars.
And scarred hands know how to hold broken stories.
They thought the pit would become Joseph's grave—but God turned the place of his rejection into a road toward the preservation of the very people who rejected him.
